Chapter 9: The Temptation of Religious Pride.
As our journey keeps moving forward, there’s a new kind of danger that starts to show up—one that’s easy to miss because it’s so subtle. It’s the temptation to measure your worth by what you do on the outside, to stack yourself up against others, or to take pride in how much you’ve given up or how obedient you’ve been. This sort of pride doesn’t shout. It just quietly slips in, and before you know it, real faith can turn into a performance.
Imagine someone who’s made tough choices, let go of comforts, and served others, day in and day out. After a while, they might start to notice where everyone else falls short. There’s this quiet sense of superiority that creeps in—the feeling that they’re doing better, or that their sacrifices somehow make them more deserving. Suddenly, the joy of the journey is replaced by this need to be recognized, to be seen as special.
And here’s the thing—most people don’t set out to be self-righteous. It just sort of happens, almost without noticing. The focus drifts from that first, genuine calling, and lands squarely on the self. Hearts start to harden. Compassion fades away. What was once sparked by love becomes just another way to chase approval.
So, what’s the antidote? It’s humility. It’s that deep-down willingness to remember that everything we have is a gift. Grace isn’t something you earn. No one is above needing forgiveness. The stories of people who have stumbled, fallen, and then found their way back? Those remind us—the journey isn’t about being perfect. It’s about learning to depend on something bigger than ourselves.
Now, humility doesn’t mean putting yourself down or pretending you’re less than you are. It’s about seeing yourself honestly—knowing your strengths, owning your weaknesses, and feeling grateful for both. It’s about celebrating when someone else grows, not just when you do. In a world that’s obsessed with climbing higher, humility is almost revolutionary.
And over time, something amazing happens for people who choose humility. The urge to compare, to compete, to be noticed—it just starts to fade. What’s left is this simple, lasting joy in the journey itself, and a deep, steady gratitude for the grace that makes every step possible.
